cards.heading: Standard vs extended
cards.body: Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match only the source address. Extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) match protocol, source, destination and optionally ports, so they can be far more precise. Neither type matches MAC addresses. In an entry, 'host 10.1.1.10' is the same as '10.1.1.10 0.0.0.0', and IOS knows common ports by name ('eq https' is 'eq 443').
cards.example:
access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 443

cards.heading: Top-down, first match wins
cards.body: The router checks a packet against each line in order. The first line that matches decides permit or deny, and the remaining lines are never checked. Put specific lines before general ones.
cards.example:
10 deny   tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.1.10 eq 22
20 permit ip  192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any
→ SSH to 10.1.1.10 is denied by 10; everything else is permitted by 20

cards.heading: The implicit deny
cards.body: Every ACL ends with an invisible 'deny any' (or 'deny ip any any'). A packet that matches no line is dropped. An ACL made only of deny lines therefore blocks everything.
cards.example:
access-list 10 deny host 192.168.1.50
(implicit) deny any   ← everyone else is blocked too!
access-list 10 permit any   ← add this to allow the rest

cards.heading: Applying and placing ACLs
cards.body: An ACL does nothing until it's applied to an interface in a direction. You can have one ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol. Place extended ACLs close to the source (drop traffic early) and standard ACLs close to the destination (they can't tell destinations apart). 'in' filters packets as they arrive on the interface, before the routing decision; 'out' filters packets about to leave it, and traffic the router generates itself isn't filtered by an outbound ACL. Applying a second ACL in the same direction replaces the first.

cards.heading: Named ACLs and sequence numbers
cards.body: Named ACLs are easier to read and let you insert or delete single lines by sequence number without retyping the whole list. In a numbered ACL, a new 'access-list 10 ...' line is appended at the bottom; to insert one elsewhere, edit it with 'ip access-list standard 10' and give a sequence number. Inside ACL configuration mode 'no 20' removes one entry, while 'no ip access-list extended BLOCK' deletes the whole ACL.
cards.example:
ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
 10 permit tcp any host 10.1.1.10 eq 443
 15 permit tcp any host 10.1.1.10 eq 80
 no 10
